title: Merged Horner
summary: The clinical presentation of Horner Syndrome accompanied by ipsilateral head, neck, or facial pain is a medical emergency. In the absence of trauma, this must be considered an Internal Carotid Artery Dissection (ICAD) until proven otherwise, carrying a significant risk of thromboembolic stroke. Navigate the intricate world of neuro-ophthalmology with this visual guide covering Horner Syndrome, Adie Pupil, Light-Near Dissociation, and Chiasmal Visual Field Defects. Understand diagnostic pathways, key clinical findings, and management protocols for these critical conditions. A high-fidelity clinical roadmap for assessing unequal pupils, ranging from physiological variations to complex sympathetic and parasympathetic chain pathologies. This guide ensures exact diagnostic protocols and investigative tables are maintained for clinical precision. A comprehensive clinical guide to diagnosing and managing oculosympathetic paresis, with a critical focus on identifying the 'Painful Horner' as a life-threatening neuro-ophthalmic emergency.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & The Triad
sections.content: Horner Syndrome (Oculosympathetic Paresis) results from a lesion anywhere along the three-neuron sympathetic pathway. The 'Painful Horner' refers to the triad of miosis, ptosis, and anhidrosis (or just miosis/ptosis) associated with acute ipsilateral cephalic or cervical pain. This presentation localizes primarily to the post-ganglionic (third-order) neuron.

sections.title: Anatomy: The 3-Neuron Pathway
content: 1st Order (Central): Hypothalamus → Ciliospinal Center of Budge (C8-T2) via brainstem.
2nd Order (Pre-ganglionic): C8-T2 → Over lung apex → Under subclavian artery → Superior Cervical Ganglion (SCG) at C2.
3rd Order (Post-ganglionic): SCG → Carotid plexus along Internal Carotid Artery (ICA) → Long ciliary nerves to Iris Dilator.
Special Note: Sudomotor fibers for the face follow the External Carotid; therefore, post-ganglionic (ICA) lesions typically SPARE facial sweating.

rows: TIA, Amaurosis fugax, CN IX-XII palsies

sections.title: The 'Ocular Triad' Exam Findings
content: Miosis: Anisocoria greater in the DARK (dilation lag).
Ptosis: Mild (1-2mm) due to paralysis of Müller's muscle.
Upside-down Ptosis: Elevation of the lower lid (paralysis of inferior tarsal muscle).
Apparent Enophthalmos: Optical illusion due to narrowed palpebral fissure.
Anhidrosis: Only present if lesion is PRE-ganglionic (1st or 2nd order).

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Immediate Referral Needed
content: Sudden onset 'worst headache of life' or neck pain.
Associated Dysphasia, Hemiparesis, or Ataxia (Stroke symptoms).
Amaurosis Fugax (Transient monocular vision loss).
Lower Cranial Nerve Palsies (Bruit, tongue deviation, dysphagia).
Acute onset Horner in the context of recent neck manipulation or minor trauma.

sections.title: Diagnostic Imaging Workflow
content: 1. Clinical Suspicion: Acute Pain + Horner.
2. Emergent Neuroimaging: CTA or MRA (Head & Neck).
3. MRI Neck with Fat Suppression: Look for 'Crescent Sign' (mural hematoma).
4. Conventional Angiography: Gold standard, but rarely needed today unless intervention planned.
5. Follow-up: Repeat imaging at 3-6 months to assess recanalization.

sections.title: Management & Treatment (ICAD)
content: Antithrombotic Therapy: Aspirin (81-325mg) or Anticoagulation (Heparin/Warfarin).
CADISS Trial: Showed no significant difference between antiplatelets and anticoagulants for stroke prevention.
Blood Pressure Management: Avoid extreme hypertension/hypotension.
Surgical/Endovascular: Stenting or bypass reserved for refractory ischemia or expanding pseudoaneurysms.

rows: Mass in Middle Cranial Fossa (Tumor, Aneurysm)
Sympathetics + CN V + multiple other CNs (III, IV, VI)

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Anhidrosis is the key differentiator: Post-ganglionic lesions (like ICAD) do NOT have facial anhidrosis.
70% of ICAD patients present with pain; Horner is only present in ~25%.
The 'Crescent Sign' on T1-weighted fat-suppressed MRI is pathognomonic for mural hematoma.
Wait at least 30-60 mins for Apraclonidine; its effect relies on denervation supersensitivity.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Stroke Risk: Highest in the first 7 days following the dissection.
Horner Resolution: Ptosis and miosis may persist indefinitely even if the artery recanalizes.
Recurrence: Low (approx 1% per year) but higher in patients with underlying connective tissue disorders (Ehlers-Danlos, FMD).

sections.title: Landmark Study: TREAT-CAD (2019)
sections.content: The TREAT-CAD trial compared Aspirin to Vitamin K Antagonists (VKA) in cervical artery dissection. It failed to prove non-inferiority of aspirin, suggesting a possible edge for anticoagulation in specific cases, though CADISS previously found them comparable. Most centers now start with Aspirin unless there is a high-grade stenosis or recurrent TIA.

sections.title: Horner Syndrome: The Oculosympathetic Pathway Unveiled
content: First order neuron =central = posterior hypothalalmus descend uncrossed down the brain stem to terminate into ciliospinal center of budge in (intermeduolateral horn of spinal cord between C8 and T2
Second order neuron (preganglionic) pass from ciliospinal center of budge to the superiocervical ganglion in neck

Third (postganglionic) ascends along the internal carotid artery to enter the cavernous sinus where it joins the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal n then it reach ciliary body and the dilator pupillae muscle via nasociliary n and the long ciliary nerves

Pharmacological tests play a crucial role in both confirming a diagnosis of Horner syndrome and localizing the lesion along the oculosympathetic pathway:
• Apraclonidine 0,5%or 1%& cocaine 4% =conﬁrm diagnosis
• Hydroxyamphetamine and adrenaline = differentiate pregaglionic from post ganglionic

sections.title: Adie Pupil: Pathophysiology & Features (Tonic Pupil)
content: Denervation of post ganglionic parasympathetic supply to sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle and may follow a viral illness
Occasionally AD
Sites of dysfunction: ciliary ganglion and in holmes adie syndrome dorsal root ganglion involved in reﬂex pathways
Female one eye though involvement of second eye typically develops within months or years
Symptoms: anisocoria, blurring of near vision
Signs:
- Large regular pupil
- Direct light reﬂex is absent or sluggish
- Vermiform movements of the pupillary border
- Constriction is also absent or sluggish in respone to light stomulation of the fellow eye (consensual)
- Pupil respond to near following wich redilatation is also slow
- Accomodation may manifest similar tonicity with slowed or impaired focusing for near and prolonged refocusing in the distance.
- Long standing cases may become small (holmes adies)
Clinical Pearl: Sector palsy of the iris sphincter is a hallmark sign, often best seen with slit lamp examination.

rows: Decrease lower limb deep tendon reﬂexes

sections.title: Adie Pupil: Diagnosis & Management
content: Pharmacological testing: 0,1-0,125% pilocarpine into both eyes leads to constrictions of abnormal pupil due to denervation hypersensitivity
Treatment if adies pupil:
- Reading glasses
- Sunglasses, low conc pilocarpine drops can be used for cosmetic reasons and to reduced photophopia
- Thoracic sympathectomy can be considered for excessive sweating

sections.title: Pharmacologically Mydriatic Eye
content: Does not constrict in bright light or on accomodation and there is no response to any concentration of pilocarpine

sections.title: Argyll Robertson Pupils: The 'Prostitute's Pupil'
content: Cause: neurosyphilis
Lesion: dorsal mid brain
Light near dissociation
Both pupils do not dilate well in dark
In bright light neither pupils constrict
On accomodation both constrict
After 0.1% pilocarpine neither pupil constricts distinguishing argyl robertson pupils from bilateral long standing tonic pupils
Clinical Pearl: Known as the 'Prostitute's Pupil' because it 'accommodates but does not react' (to light), a mnemonic from historical medical teaching.

content: 1- Observation: silent tumour
2- Medical therapy : initial step and reduction in tumour size and secretion ( cabergoline- older promocriptin- somatostatin analogue octeriotide + supplementary hormonal correction as appropriate)
3- Surgery: transsphenoidal tumour debulking
4- Radiotherapy: sterotactic radiotherapy
5- Monitoring: serial assessment of visual function

sections.title: Initial Assessment & History
content: Assessing unequal pupils begins with a detailed history, including when and who noticed the difference in pupil size.
Identify whether there are associated ophthalmic or neurological symptoms.
Review any previous ophthalmic history.
Review systemic history (see also E Anisocoria, pp. 990–1).
Investigations: See E Pupil examination, p. 31.

branches: Sympathetic chain pathology (see E Anisocoria: sympathetic chain, pp. 796–7)
Parasympathetic chain pathology (see E Anisocoria: parasympathetic chain, p. 800)

sections.title: Iris & Pharmacological Pathology
content: Iris Pathology: 2° to intraocular surgery or trauma.
Pharmacological Anisocoria: Due to local instillation/inoculation (inadvertent or intentional).
Clinical features: Fixed large (parasympathetic agents) or fixed small pupils.
Unreactive to light or accommodation.
Clinically isolated, with no associated ptosis or ocular motility problems. (Anisocoria 795)

sections.title: Pharmacological Investigations
content: Dilated pupils: Instil 1% pilocarpine, wait for 45min. Pharmacological anisocoria is confirmed when there is refusal to fully constrict.
Constricted pupils: Instil 1% tropicamide, wait for 45min. Pharmacological anisocoria is confirmed when there is refusal to fully dilate.

sections.title: Anisocoria: Sympathetic Chain (Horner’s Syndrome)
sections.content: The ocular sympathetic supply may be damaged anywhere along its route. The extent of sympathetic dysfunction, associated neurological signs, and pharmacological tests help to identify the level of the injury (796 Chapter 16 Neuro-ophthalmology).

sections.title: Horner’s Clinical Features
content: Pupil is miotic, with normal light and near reaction.
Anisocoria is most marked in dim conditions.
Ptosis and apparent enophthalmos (due to 1–2mm upper lid ptosis and 1mm elevation of lower lid).
dIOP and conjunctival injection.
Facial anhidrosis: Suggests lesion of the first- or second-order neurone.
Iris hypochromia: Suggests a congenital lesion (also in long-standing acquired lesions).

branches: Cranial Nerves: IIn (fields, discs), IIIn, IVn, Vn, VIn
History: Pain (headache, neck, arm), Trauma, Surgery

rows: Weak α1-agonist. Measure sizes at 0/60min in identical ambient lighting (bright/dim).
Blocks noradrenaline reuptake. Measure at 0/60min. Repeat at 1min. (Seldom performed).
Identify level (seldom performed). Normal dilation = 1st/2nd order lesion. No/poor dilation = 3rd order.
Not reliable if within 48h of cocaine test.

sections.title: Identify Cause & Level
sections.content: Identify cause: further investigation is directed by the likely cause and level of lesion (see Tables 16.21 and 16.22). Identify if congenital or acquired: old photographs may show changes to be long-standing (view with a 20D to see pupils); also look for additional clinical features (see E Congenital Horner’s syndrome, p. 797).

sections.title: Treatment and Prognosis
content: Dependent on underlying cause; may involve urgent referral to other specialties.
Recovery of Horner’s depends on cause and treatment.
Cluster headaches (Raeder syndrome): recovery may occur within a few hours.
Invasive tumours: may cause relentless, irreversible progression.

sections.title: Congenital Horner’s Syndrome
content: Usually idiopathic but can be 2° to birth trauma (e.g. forceps delivery).
Miosis, ptosis, and apparent enophthalmos.
Heterochromia: lighter iris pigmentation on ipsilateral side.
Facial flushing (‘harlequin’ sign): pale on affected side; seen on cycloplegic refraction or crying due to ipsilateral anhidrosis.

sections.title: CRITICAL CAUTION
content: Acquired Horner’s syndrome in childhood should be investigated for neuroblastoma.

rows: CXR, CT thorax, Carotid Doppler, MRI/ MRA head/ neck, Lymph node (LN) biopsy
Carotid Doppler, MRI/ MRA head/ neck, MRI orbits, ENT assessment
Trauma, Surgery, Tumour (thyroid, cervical LN), CCA dissection

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Horner Syndrome (oculosympathetic paresis) results from an interruption of the sympathetic nerve supply to the eye and adnexa. It is classically defined by the triad of miosis, ptosis, and anhidrosis. While often benign, its sudden onset—especially when accompanied by pain—can signal life-threatening conditions such as internal carotid artery dissection (ICAD) or Pancoast tumor.

sections.title: The Three-Order Neuron Pathway
content: 1st Order (Central): Hypothalamus → Ciliospinal Center of Budge (C8-T2). Passes through the brainstem.
2nd Order (Pre-ganglionic): Ciliospinal Center → Over the Lung Apex → Superior Cervical Ganglion (Level of Mandible/C2).
3rd Order (Post-ganglionic): Superior Cervical Ganglion → Carotid Plexus → Through Cavernous Sinus → Long Ciliary Nerves → Iris Dilator & Müller's Muscle.

rows: Pancoast Tumor (Lung), Thoracic Aneurysm, Birth Trauma (Klumpke), Iatrogenic (Surgery)
Arm pain, hand muscle wasting (T1 involvement)
Carotid Dissection, Cluster Headache, Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis, Raeder Syndrome

sections.title: The Painful Horner: RED ALERTS
content: Internal Carotid Artery Dissection (ICAD) until proven otherwise.
Acute onset of facial, neck, or periorbital pain.
Amaurosis Fugax or TIA-like symptoms.
History of minor neck trauma (e.g., yoga, chiropractic, coughing).
Associated CN XII palsy (suggests extracranial CAD).

sections.title: Clinical Signs & Ocular Findings
content: Miosis: Anisocoria is greater in the dark (dilation lag).
Ptosis: Mild (1-2mm) due to Müller's muscle weakness.
Upside-down Ptosis: Elevation of the lower eyelid.
Anhidrosis: Loss of sweating (Total face: 1st order; Forehead only: 3rd order).
Iris Heterochromia: If congenital (affected eye is lighter).
Apparent Enophthalmos: Due to narrow palpebral fissure.

sections.title: Pharmacological Testing Protocol
content: Step 1: Apraclonidine 0.5% or 1% (Diagnosis). Horner pupil dilates; normal pupil does not (reversal of anisocoria).
Step 2: Cocaine 4% or 10% (Gold Standard Diagnosis). Horner pupil fails to dilate; normal pupil dilates.
Step 3: Hydroxyamphetamine 1% (Localization). Dilates 1st/2nd order; fails to dilate 3rd order.
Step 4: Phenylephrine 1% (3rd order check). Significant dilation suggests 3rd order due to denervation supersensitivity.

branches: Dark > Light (Sympathetic): Horner, Physiological Anisocoria, Long-standing Argyll Robertson
Light > Dark (Parasympathetic): Adie Tonic Pupil, CN III Palsy, Pharmacological Mydriasis, Trauma/Sphincter Damage

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Strategy
content: 1. Confirm Diagnosis (Apraclonidine/Cocaine test).
2. Determine Urgency: If PAINFUL → Immediate ER referral for MRA Head/Neck.
3. Localize: Check for associated CN palsies or 'long-tract' signs.
4. Imaging: MRI Brain, MRA/CTA Head & Neck, CT/X-ray Chest (Apex).

content.explanation: Ptosis, Anhidrosis, and Miosis = Horner Syndrome.

sections.title: Imaging Specifics for CAD
content: Axial T1 with FAT SATURATION is the gold standard for detecting intramural hematoma.
MRA or CTA of the neck must include the 'carotid string sign'.
Scan from the Arch of the Aorta to the Circle of Willis.

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
content: Most common cause: Birth trauma (brachial plexus injury).
Crucial Red Flag: Neuroblastoma (must check urinary catecholamines/VMA).
Characteristic Sign: Iris heterochromia (hypochromia on the affected side).

sections.title: Surgical Management
content: Müller Muscle Conjunctival Resection (MMCR): For correcting the mild ptosis.
Fasanella-Servat Procedure: A variation of MMCR often used.
Levator Aponeurosis Advancement: Reserved for larger ptosis components.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls (High Yield)
content: Dilation Lag: The anisocoria is most prominent 5 seconds after lights out.
Wallenberg Syndrome: Expect ipsilateral Horner + contralateral loss of pain/temp.
Apraclonidine False Negative: May occur in very acute cases (<48 hours) due to lack of receptor upregulation.

sections.title: Landmark Studies: The 'Pain' Evidence
sections.content: A landmark study by Biousse et al. noted that Horner syndrome occurs in approximately 25% to 58% of internal carotid artery dissections. In many cases, it is the *only* presenting sign before a major stroke occurs. Immediate anticoagulation or antiplatelet therapy is often required once the dissection is confirmed by imaging.

sections.title: Summary of Complications
content: Ischemic Stroke (if CAD is missed).
Metastatic spread of occult malignancy (Pancoast tumor).
Permanent ocular cosmetic defects (ptosis).
Progression of underlying neurological disease (MS/Tumor).
